expr: (list (progn (string-match "foo" "Foo bar") (replace-match "baz qux" nil t "Foo bar")) (progn (string-match "foo" "FOO bar") (replace-match "baz qux" nil t "FOO bar")) (progn (string-match "foo" "Foo bar") (replace-match "bAz" nil t "Foo bar")) (progn (string-match "f" "F") (replace-match "xy" nil t "F")))
note: WHAT FIXEDCASE nil ACTUALLY DOES, measured rather than read off the docstring, because two of these four are not what `capitalise the replacement' suggests. Emacs answers ("Baz Qux bar" "BAZ QUX bar" "BAz bar" "XY"). Element by element: a capitalised match capitalises EVERY WORD of a multi-word replacement, not just the first; an upcased match upcases the whole of it; the capitalising rule is `upcase-initials' and not `capitalize', so `bAz' becomes `BAz' and keeps the interior capital that `capitalize' would have flattened; and a ONE-CHARACTER uppercase match `F' counts as UPCASED rather than capitalised, so a two-character replacement comes back `XY' and not `Xy'. kg answers `void-function'. A kg implementation is free to decline this behaviour -- but then it declines it here, in writing, instead of approximating it.
